name: Rafael Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say to colleagues and what you think privately. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Rafael, 43, and I lead a team that writes route software for a waste-collection company. I have a master’s degree and I’m good at finding why a route sent a truck down a closed street. I start with missed-pickup reports, check the driver’s notes and review code before a new route is sent. I use AI now and then to summarise incident reports after a colleague tested it, but I verify each street change on the map.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much does your family depend on this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Nia, does accounts for a small supplier, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My developer pay is typical, and we have about three months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby. Nia’s hours change at month-end, so we plan the bills around the lower number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau leaves drivers and developers checking the actual street before a route changes. A quick incident summary is useful, but a truck still needs a road it can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel steady about my job. Three months saved covers a short gap, though Nia’s variable accounting hours keep the mortgage budget tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep matching AI incident summaries with driver notes and the street map. I’d move 160 monthly into savings only when Nia’s hours cover the planned bills. In the first year I’d ask drivers to mark every new road closure before a software route goes live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the household, not my code job. A lower accounting month still changes what we can save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which route mistake stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A truck was sent to a street blocked by building work, and its driver lost an hour turning around. I found the blocked-street closure in a handwritten driver note our route map missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about a low accounting month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Nia we can keep our current budget and pause the children’s extra weekend activity only if her hours actually fall. We would decide after the payslip, not before.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking streets before routes change.
I would keep **driver notes** beside incident summaries.
think: I expect my **developer job** to hold.
I worry Nia’s **variable hours** can still squeeze the mortgage budget.
do: **Keep** matching AI summaries with driver notes and street maps.
**Save** 160 monthly only when Nia’s hours cover bills.
**Ask drivers** to mark road closures before release; pause children’s extra weekend activity only if Nia’s hours fall.
feel: **Uneasy** about household hours, with my job stable.
S0.quote: I found the blocked-street closure in a handwritten driver note our route map missed.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** is checked against real street maps and handwritten driver notes after a missed closure.
A **three-month reserve** helps, but Nia’s variable hours govern the savings transfer.

steps.text: Check summaries against driver notes; ask drivers to mark road closures before release
Save 160 monthly only when accounting hours cover bills
Pause children’s extra weekend activity only if Nia’s paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let AI plan routes, draft code and answer missed-pickup calls faster. I would ask drivers to test routes before management cuts the review time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry one lead could be asked to cover the work of two developers. Nia’s account checks may also be automated, so we could feel pressure on both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d test the approved route planner against twelve old road-closure incidents with a driver this month. If it avoids all twelve, I’d learn to inspect its proposals during paid time. In the first year, if our team is reduced, I’d attend the workers’ council with the drivers to ask for safe route checks and notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about household pay, even though I can learn the tool. Three months saved is not long if both jobs lose hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the workers’ council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the blocked-street case to the council and ask how many driver minutes the new target allows for checking. A fast route that misses a closure simply moves the delay onto the driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Nia about her work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Nia what parts of her accounts job are actually changing. I would not count a rumour about software as a lost shift yet.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed routes, code and pickup replies.
I would demand **driver-tested routes** before review time is cut.
think: I fear a **smaller developer team** could cut my hours.
I worry Nia’s **account checks** could shrink at the same time.
do: **Test** an approved route planner against twelve old road closures.
**Learn** to inspect its proposals during paid time only if all twelve are avoided.
**Attend** the workers’ council if the developer team is reduced.
feel: **Anxious** about two possible wage cuts despite a three-month cushion.
S1.quote: A fast route that misses a closure simply moves the delay onto the driver.
fieldNote: He accepts a **twelve-closure trial** before reducing driver review or learning a new planner.
His **council action** depends on team reductions and combines driver safety with staffing notice.

steps.text: Learn approved route planning during paid time if twelve closures are avoided
Attend workers council if developer team is reduced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches route-code and accounting thinking work by 2028. Hands-on collection robots arrive around 2031, but neither my desk nor Nia’s account screen gets that delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer role could go and Nia’s hours could fall. Three months saved will not carry two lost wages and a mortgage through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask both employers for written staffing and severance terms now. I’d hold off on the planned family holiday deposit and keep the money for the mortgage. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for actual local openings and eligible income help, while Nia checks her own hours before we change the whole budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect a big cut to our income. A family holiday deposit will not protect the children’s school travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the holiday is delayed, not cancelled forever. We would keep school travel and meals first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the workers’ council help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the workers’ council to compare severance offers if several developers are cut. We could make a group request for paid transition time instead of signing separately.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach route code and accounting before robots arrive.
I would stress **both desk incomes** face the earlier date.
think: I expect my **developer role** could end and Nia’s hours could fall.
Our **three-month savings** cannot carry two lost wages through a mortgage.
do: **Delay** the family holiday and hold its deposit for the mortgage.
**Request** written staffing terms and group transition time if several developers are cut.
**Apply** for actual local jobs and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
S2.quote: A family holiday deposit will not protect the children’s school travel.
fieldNote: Both adults face **thinking-work change** in 2028; later collection robots add little time to their screen work.
The **council request** needs group cuts, while public help and new work depend on eligibility and vacancies.

steps.text: Delay family holiday and hold deposit for mortgage bills
Ask workers council for group transition terms if several developers are cut
Apply for actual local jobs if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn how drivers handle closed streets before thinking AI reaches our code. Collection robots arrive around 2034, later than the route-planning change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer code roles, but I could learn driver operations while earning. I cannot assume on-site detour work stays paid once collection robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for one approved morning monthly with a driver learning how detours are checked on site. I’d use the free safety manual if the company refuses the time. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d apply for actual operations-support openings only if their pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my job, with time to test a real skill. I would keep the three-month reserve for bills rather than buy a course on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove an operations skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the driver to mark one detour report I wrote each month. If my route sends a truck into a narrow street, I need more practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a certificate unless a real opening requires it and we can afford it. The free manual and an approved morning should tell me whether I can do the work.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to learn real detour checks.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier route-code change.
think: I expect **fewer coding roles** despite five years of warning.
I cannot assume **field operations** stays paid once robots arrive.
do: **Learn detour checks** one approved morning monthly and have a driver mark my report.
**Study** the free safety manual if approved time is refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying operations jobs if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about route-code work, with time for an evidence-led trial.
S3.quote: I cannot assume on-site detour work stays paid once collection robots arrive.
fieldNote: His **field trial** needs approved work time, with a free safety manual instead of costly speculative tuition.
The **operations search** requires real openings and mortgage-covering pay.

steps.text: Learn detours one approved morning monthly with driver feedback; otherwise study free manual
Apply after 2031 coding loss for real operations jobs covering mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to make routes safer and train drivers on new maps. Thinking AI reaches code and accounting in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect both wages to hold for now, though Nia’s hours can still vary. I want the route team to keep real driver feedback in its work even if the software gets faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing route changes with driver notes and save 160 monthly when Nia’s hours cover bills. I’d ask the workers’ council to review route-check time each year. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d search actual local openings and compare pay before considering a family move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, while the mortgage looks manageable today. I can use the decade without treating it as a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the blocked-street note to the council and ask whether drivers have enough time to flag a bad route. I would not call a waste route safe just because the software met its speed target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia and I would keep the children at their present school unless a real offer pays for a move. We would compare mortgage and travel costs before telling them.

I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code shift.
think: I expect **both wages** to hold in the near term.
I want **driver feedback** protected even as route software speeds up.
do: **Keep** checking driver notes and save 160 monthly when Nia’s hours cover bills.

feel: **Uneasy** about long-term work, with current mortgage bills manageable.
S4.quote: I would not call a waste route safe just because the software met its speed target.
fieldNote: He uses the **decade** for driver feedback and careful spending while wages continue.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code and Nia’s account checks could shrink together. Written severance, paid time to learn operations and income help we qualify for would help. Three months of savings buys a few decisions, not two new wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who speaks to the driver when a neat route map sends a truck to a closed street. A missed waste pickup leaves a person outside waiting with the bin.

headlineQuote: A missed waste pickup leaves a person outside waiting with the bin.
portrait: Rafael is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree and strong skill in waste-collection routes.
He uses **AI occasionally** for incident summaries, checking results against driver notes and real road closures.
His partner’s **accounting work** faces thinking AI alongside his code, while variable hours already affect the mortgage budget.
He seeks **driver-tested tools**, council input, approved operations learning and actual jobs paying enough for the family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut both route-code pay and accounting hours before their three-month reserve grows.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid operations learning and eligible income help would support the family.
